MCV is the primary reference; the others describe velocity, range and duration.
How stable velocity is obtained without directly subtracting consecutive frames.
Only valid repetitions contribute to best MCV and velocity loss. Uncertain and invalid repetitions remain visible for review.
This analysis does not estimate force, power, 1RM or fatigue. Accuracy depends on framing, calibration, tracking and video continuity.
The known length is divided by the actual distance occupied by points A and B in the image.
Lref: known length · dAB: distance between A and B
Distance A B is the square root of the horizontal difference squared plus the vertical difference squared. Scale is the reference length divided by distance A B.
Places the origin at the first tracked point and makes upward movement positive.
X keeps the image direction. Y is inverted so upward movement has a positive sign.
s: metric scale · subscript 0: initial position · px: pixels
The x coordinate is the horizontal pixel difference multiplied by scale. The y coordinate is the initial vertical position minus the current vertical position, multiplied by scale.
Reconstructs real time from video PTS.
The first PTS sets the time origin. In slow motion, the interval is divided by the automatically inferred factor; without evidence, real time is used.
PTSi: frame timestamp · fslow: slow-motion factor
Physical frame time is its PTS minus the initial PTS, divided by the slow-motion factor.
Primary metric of the concentric phase.
Total vertical displacement during the upward phase divided by its duration.
c: concentric phase · start: beginning · end: finish
MCV is the final upward position minus the initial position, divided by final time minus initial time.
Highest processed velocity during the upward phase.
The maximum smoothed velocity is used, never raw differences. It is reliable from 119.5 fps; between 59.5 and 119.5 fps it is marked low confidence, and below that it is not reported.
c: upward-phase samples · v with hat: processed velocity
PV is the maximum processed vertical velocity during the concentric phase.
Distance between the repetition’s vertical extremes.
The lowest processed position is subtracted from the highest within the repetition.
r: repetition samples · y with hat: processed position
ROM is the maximum processed vertical position minus the minimum processed vertical position of the repetition.
Duration of the concentric and eccentric phases.
Each duration is the difference between the final and initial time of its phase.
Tc: concentric time · Te: eccentric time
Concentric time is the end minus the start of the upward phase. Eccentric time is the end minus the start of the downward phase.
Stopped time at the change of direction.
One normal frame interval is subtracted and the result can never be negative.
phase 1: first phase · phase 2: second phase · Δt with tilde: median frame interval
Pause is the maximum of zero and the start of the second phase minus the end of the first phase minus the median frame interval.
Mean velocity of the eccentric phase.
It is calculated like MCV, but over the downward phase. Its value is negative because descending corresponds to −Y.
e: eccentric phase · start: beginning · end: finish
MEV is the final downward position minus the initial position, divided by final time minus initial time.
Compares each valid repetition with the previous or current best.
Bᵢ is the best valid MCV through repetition i. A new best has 0% loss.
𝒱ᵢ: valid repetitions through i · Bᵢ: best MCV in that set
B sub i is the best MCV among valid repetitions through i. Velocity loss is one hundred times B sub i minus the current MCV, divided by B sub i.
How the trajectory is smoothed without raw differences.
A local polynomial is fitted with confidence-squared weights. Vertical velocity is its analytical derivative at the central frame.
z: normalized local time · hi: window time scale · a: fitted coefficients
Processed vertical position is fitted with a local cubic polynomial. Vertical velocity at the central frame is coefficient a one divided by the window time scale.

They use the available weight and/or stature captured when the athlete was assigned or reassigned. Ordinary video does not directly measure power, force or impulse; measuring force or impulse requires a force plate or other validated instrumentation.
Estimated peak power (Sayers): P = 60.7 × jump height (cm) + 45.3 × mass (kg) − 2055. Relative power: relative P = P / mass.
Potential energy: PE = m × g × h. Vertical kinetic energy at takeoff: KE = ½ × m × v². Vertical momentum at takeoff: p = m × v.
Percent-of-stature scores are descriptive normalizations, not power or force measures, and do not fully remove body-size effects.
The app uses g = 9.80665 m/s². Flight-time height assumes ballistic motion and equal center-of-mass height at takeoff and landing. Energy and momentum approximate vertical center-of-mass motion.

Sayers is shown only for SJ and CMJ. For the closest protocol match, keep the hands on the waist. It was derived with SJ, and the study reported a 2.7% overestimate when applied to CMJ. Accuracy is not established for children, clinical populations, unusual body sizes, or populations unlike the validation sample.
Source: Sayers et al. (1999) · open DOI

How OpenJump protects your data and videos

OpenJump has no account or OpenJump server and does not request Internet permission; core processing runs on this device. Copies can leave the app/device when you choose to create, share, export, or send a support email. Destination apps or services may handle or sync those copies.

Saved records in OpenJump’s private app storage can include athlete names and optional birth date, sex, notes, weight and height, plus jump/Encoder results and analysis. A record may keep a reference URI for a selected video; the video bytes are not copied into the database.

Recordings are published to shared Movies/OpenJump, where other apps may access or sync them. Imported videos are read from your selected location, not copied into the database; a saved record may retain only its URI reference. Deleting a result does not delete the video. Delete shared videos separately in a gallery or file manager.

OpenJump has no automatic analytics/telemetry or backend. You can explicitly save a recording to shared Movies/OpenJump, export JSON/CSV or a trajectory video, or create manual backup v1; the backup is not encrypted or authenticated and a chosen provider may sync it. About can open an editable email draft to openjump.app@gmail.com with app version/code and Android release/API, manufacturer and model, plus blank issue prompts. It does not auto-attach IDs, account data, videos, results, paths or URIs and does not send the draft. Review/edit it and choose whether to send in your email app; you may add personal information. The email app/provider handles a sent message. About also lets you choose to copy the same basic installation/device diagnostics above to the clipboard or share them with an app you choose through Android\'s chooser.

Saved records remain in private app storage until you delete them or clear app data/uninstall. Archiving an athlete retains history. Android cloud backup/device transfer are disabled. Exports, manual backups, shared videos and email messages you chose to send are separate copies; manage or delete them with their destination app/provider. A backup v1 file is plaintext and unauthenticated and may be synchronized by its provider.

The camera is used only when you choose to record. Android 8 and 9 require legacy storage write access to publish recordings to Movies/OpenJump; newer versions use scoped media storage. OpenJump does not request Internet, microphone or location permission. It is a sports-performance tool, not a clinical or diagnostic tool.

OpenJump source code is published at github.com/cortig00/OpenJump under the GPL-3.0-or-later license. You may study, modify, and redistribute it under that license. Official releases are distributed through Google Play and channels linked from the repository.
Questions, or want to request deletion of a support message you chose to send? Contact openjump.app@gmail.com. No specific message-retention period or automatic deletion is promised.

Experimental F–V–P estimate — simplified Samozino/Morin method

Force, velocity and power are model estimates from jump height, total mass and measured push-off distance. F0 and V0 are extrapolated theoretical intercepts; Pmax is the maximum of the fitted model. This workflow has not yet been validated with real multi-load series.
A high R² does not establish measurement validity or the accuracy of extrapolated intercepts.
Flight-time height assumes comparable body posture at takeoff and landing. Countermovement in SJ, arm swing, inconsistent depth, load movement or an altered landing posture can bias the estimate.
Measure how far the same body landmark rises from crouch to extended tiptoe stance, without leaving the ground. This is not jump height and is not calculated from stature.
The push-off distance is approximated by measuring the displacement of the chosen landmark: it is a field approximation, not a direct measurement of the center of mass.
What it is: we estimate how force and velocity relate when jumping with different loads.
What you need: body mass, push-off distance and jumps with different loads.
Limit: an experimental estimate, not a direct measurement or training recommendation.
In per-condition mode, push-off distance is declared for each condition in Jumps.
Field approximation: not jump height or a direct measurement of centre-of-mass displacement.

Diagram of two positions with the feet on the ground: crouch on the left and extended tiptoe on the right. The same anatomical mark appears in both positions and a vertical arrow joins their heights: that distance is h_po. The diagram does not show free flight, does not use stature and does not calculate the centre of mass.

Keep both feet on the ground and choose a point you can always feel in the same place. Mark its height in the crouch and in the extended tiptoe position: h_po is the vertical distance between the two marks. It is not jump height during flight, it is not estimated from stature and no centre of mass is calculated: it is a field approximation.
